clue.text: Wolves regularly circling after playing with a small creature

indicators.note: circling means going around, so the selected letters wrap around the reworked word
taking things at regular intervals means keeping every other letter of the team name

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters of the club's name

indicators.note: a word that is playing about is not keeping still, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Wolverhampton Wanderers keep circling after kicking a ball about with a small pet.
explanation.walkthrough: Wolves is Wolverhampton Wanderers, an English football club. W_LE goes round ATERF, then A ends it: WATER FLEA.
explanation.definitionFit: A water flea, or daphnia, is a tiny crustacean living in ponds, so it is a little animal.

clue.text: Lift half a bottle?

indicators.note: only half of the vessel's name is wanted, so its second five letters are dropped

parts.note: a Winchester is a large glass bottle, typically holding two and a half litres

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person who swiped half a bottle of drink has 'lifted' it.
explanation.walkthrough: A Winchester (bottle) has ten letters; the front half is WINCH. 'Lift' suggests stealing, but here it means hoist.
explanation.definitionFit: To winch something is to haul or hoist it upwards with a cable wound on a drum.

clue.text: Ralph Richardson's initial put, how funny!

indicators.note: funny suggests something odd or peculiar, so the letters come out in a strange order
an initial is the opening letter of a name, so only the surname's first letter is used

parts.note: first letter of the actor's surname
taken as written, ready for rearranging

explanation.surface: A comment on how amusingly the great actor Sir Ralph Richardson delivered a line.
explanation.walkthrough: The actor's first name is the definition: 'ralph' is slang for vomiting.
explanation.definitionFit: To ralph is a slang verb for being sick, imitating the sound of retching, so it matches throwing up.

clue.text: See 6 Across
Toll reduced for Spooner, 18 at Agincourt?

indicators.note: Spooner was the Oxford don famous for swapping the opening sounds of neighbouring words

parts.note: a bell's toll is a bong; swapped starts give the first word
reduced means brought low; swapped starts give the second word

explanation.surface: A price cut at a toll booth, oddly attributed to Spooner and to the battle of Agincourt.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 down is SHOOTER. BONG LOW swaps its initial sounds to LONG BOW.
explanation.definitionFit: English archers at Agincourt in 1415 shot with the longbow, the weapon that won the battle.

clue.text: Huge winger's heavy weight?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an enormous seabird with the largest wingspan of any bird
second meaning: a burden one cannot shake off, from Coleridge's Ancient Mariner

explanation.surface: A large footballer on the wing, described as a heavyweight.
explanation.walkthrough: Winger sounds like a footballer but means anything with wings. In Coleridge's poem the mariner must wear the bird he killed round his neck, hence a burden.
explanation.definitionFit: The great seabird has a vast wingspan, and figuratively it names a burdensome encumbrance or curse.

clue.text: Number near four grasped by cow

indicators.note: something grasped is held inside, so the animal's word goes round the rest

parts.note: a cow is something that moos

explanation.surface: A figure next to four is being held by a cow, like a farmyard counting game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks numerical but means a song. NRIV sits inside MOO_ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Moon River is the Henry Mancini song from Breakfast at Tiffany's, and a song is a musical number.

clue.text: Resort where horse pierced by 18

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing pushed through its middle, so the horse word is split open

parts.note: 18 down is shooter, a gun, and gat is slang for a gun

explanation.surface: A seaside resort where a horse is wounded by a gunman.
explanation.walkthrough: Margate is a seaside town in Kent. 18 points to SHOOTER, so the solver needs a synonym for it: GAT inside MAR_E.
explanation.definitionFit: Margate is a traditional English seaside holiday town, a classic resort for day trippers from London.

clue.text: Flog patent with deposit of English king

indicators.note: having something with it here means the open adjective holds the royal letters inside

parts.note: patent in the sense of plain and open
read as deposed: a former ruler is an ex
R for rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: Someone sells off a patent along with an English king's deposit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deposit' is read as 'deposed', giving EX; EX E R, a deposed English king, sits inside OVER_T.
explanation.definitionFit: To flog oneself or a horse is to drive it too hard, which is to overexert it.

clue.text: Hypothetical splashing of urn across pressure cooker

indicators.note: lying across something means spanning it, so the rearranged letters straddle the single letter
splashing liquid flies about in disorder, so the vessel's letters are scattered

explanation.surface: A tea urn spilling over a pressure cooker in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pressure cooker' reads as one kitchen gadget, but it splits into two parts: a physics symbol and a separate appliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hypothetical is supposed but not yet demonstrated, so it remains without proof.

clue.text: Dog kennels new realm for 12

indicators.note: to kennel is to house a dog inside a shelter, so the dog word encloses the rest
a new version is a remade one, so the letters are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A dog houses a new kingdom, a fanciful image of a dog's own domain.
explanation.walkthrough: 12 across is COOPER, so the definition is a cooper. RELMA sits inside BAR_KER.
explanation.definitionFit: A cooper is a craftsman who builds wooden casks and barrels, so the trade name is a barrel maker.

clue.text: See 22
'Rat', and translated into 'donkey'

indicators.note: into means going inside, so the translated word is put within the animal word

parts.note: a donkey is something that brays

explanation.surface: A word, Rat, gets translated into donkey, as in a children's language game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'And translated' is French et, placed after the B of BRAYER. 'And' does double duty here as part of the fragment; the comma-free reading is 'and, translated, into donkey'.
explanation.definitionFit: A rat in slang is someone who deserts or informs on his friends, which is a betrayer.

clue.text: Potion originally drunk by pigeon for Alice, say?

indicators.note: something drunk ends up inside the drinker, so the bird word swallows the letter
originally points to the very beginning, so only the opening letter of the drink word counts

explanation.surface: Like Alice in Wonderland, someone drinks a potion, though here a pigeon does the drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: The Wonderland potion is a decoy: the Alice wanted is the shock-rock singer Alice Cooper.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Cooper is the American rock singer, so he is one example of somebody bearing that surname.

clue.text: Vessel at end of channel tipped up to feed pig

indicators.note: feeding puts food into an animal, so these letters go inside the pig word
in a down clue tipping something up stands it on its head, so it reads backwards
the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A boat at the end of a canal is capsized while feeding a pig, a muddled farmyard scene.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'tipped up' reads from the bottom upwards; 'channel' is not a waterway here but just supplies its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An oil tanker is a large ship built to carry crude oil, so it is a seagoing vessel.

clue.text: Natural park, a tip I found in it

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so these words sit within the park

parts.note: short for recreation ground, a public park
to tip is to lean or list

explanation.surface: A naturalist's park where someone discovers a rubbish tip.
explanation.walkthrough: A rec is British shorthand for a recreation ground, a local park. A LIST I goes inside RE_C.
explanation.definitionFit: Realistic art or acting looks natural, true to life rather than stylised.

clue.text: Western residence, minister recalled, for anybody

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the clergyman's abbreviation comes back to front

explanation.surface: A western house where the vicar has been recalled, open to anybody.
explanation.walkthrough: REV, the reverend, is reversed to VER at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Whomever means any person at all, used as the object of a verb, so it can stand for anybody.

clue.text: Muzzles worn by boy with right outfit

indicators.note: something worn is put on around the wearer, so the gags enclose the boy

explanation.surface: A boy wearing a muzzle with the correct costume, perhaps for a dog-themed party.
explanation.walkthrough: LAD and R, the boy with right, sit inside G_AGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Glad rags is an informal idiom for one's best clothes, worn for a party: a smart outfit.

clue.text: A body for modelling permissible in journal

indicators.note: modelling is shaping material like clay into a new form, so the letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Whether a body for life modelling is acceptable to describe in a diary.
explanation.definitionFit: A daybook is a diary or book of accounts where each day's events are recorded, so a journal.

clue.text: Owl after small piece

explanation.surface: An owl coming after a small piece of food, like a bird of prey's snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts HOOTER behind S. 'Piece' is slang for a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are gangster slang for a handgun: a piece is a firearm, and so is a shooter.

clue.text: Ultimately, gnats and bats like Bengal cats?

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the insects is taken

parts.note: bats and potty both mean crazy

explanation.surface: A pest-ridden night where gnats and bats bother Bengal cats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' looks like the flying animals but is the adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Bengal cats are a breed with leopard-like markings, so their coats are covered in spots.

clue.text: Apparent, circulating roll of banknotes should feature head of royal

parts.note: something circulating, like news, is out

indicators.note: a thing that features something includes it, so the roll of notes holds the royal letter
head of picks out the opening letter, which is then placed inside

parts.note: a wad is a thick roll of notes

explanation.surface: Circulating banknotes ought to carry the monarch's head, as British notes do.
explanation.walkthrough: R sits inside WA_D after OUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Outward describes how things seem on the surface, so outward signs are apparent ones.

clue.text: Boy in a crib discontented after spilling child's drink

indicators.note: what is spilt lands in a jumble, so these letters are mixed up
without its contents a word keeps only its outside letters

explanation.surface: An unhappy boy in his cot after knocking over a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' looks like unhappy but means emptied, leaving CB.
explanation.definitionFit: A babycino is frothed milk in a cup, served in cafes so a child can copy adults drinking cappuccino.

clue.text: Cat catching 18 out, heavenly sight

indicators.note: a cat catching prey holds it, so the cat word wraps around the rest
out here means put out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 18 down, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A cat catching a gunman would be a heavenly sight indeed.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 down is SHOOTER; its letters go inside ME_WER.
explanation.definitionFit: A meteor shower is a display of many shooting stars streaking across the night sky, a celestial spectacle.

clue.text: See 9 Across
Letters from author a template for lecture

indicators.note: letters drawn from a phrase are a consecutive run sitting inside it

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the words

explanation.surface: An author using a set form letter as a template for a talk.
explanation.walkthrough: The run starts at the end of 'author' and stops early in 'template'.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to speak at length in a formal, often pompous manner, as in giving a lecture.

clue.text: Make last dance work: the tango you suspect last of all?

indicators.note: the last of every word means taking the final letter from each one in turn

parts.words: dance work: the tango you suspect

explanation.surface: A dancer asks for help making a tango routine work, suspecting it needs stretching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' appears twice: once in the definition as a verb meaning endure, once in the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out supplies is to stretch them so they go further, making them last longer.

clue.text: Short dash for food delivery?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a short dash is the minus sign, read as subtract
second meaning: a meal bought hot to be eaten elsewhere

explanation.walkthrough: The minus sign is a short dash, and children call subtraction 'take away'. In Britain a takeaway is what Americans call takeout.
explanation.definitionFit: The minus sign is spoken as take away in sums, and a takeaway is a cooked meal collected or delivered.

clue.text: Journey of hiker traipsing about?

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the run is read backwards
made of means drawn from within, so the letters lie inside the following words

parts.note: a run straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A walker trudging around on a long hike.
explanation.definitionFit: A trek is a long, arduous trip, especially one made on foot, so it is a journey.

clue.text: Case where filth ending in slammer, put back in prison

indicators.note: in means inside, so the turned letters go within the prison word
putting something back returns it the other way round
ending in tells us the dirt is followed by the last letter of the jail word

explanation.surface: A legal case in which the filth, British slang for police, end up in the slammer themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Filth' hints at the police but just means dirt. DIRT plus R is reversed inside CA_GE.
explanation.definitionFit: A cartridge is a casing holding ink, film or a bullet's charge, so it is a case.
